soil-properties-s1.title: Four soil samples on the soil texture triangle

soil-properties-s2.title: A class tests how water moves through three soils

table.caption: Each soil: a 10 cm deep column, 200 mL of water poured on top (invented data for practice)
cols: Time for the water to pass through the column (minutes)

items.q: Which list puts soil particles in order from largest to smallest?
options: Sand, silt, clay
Clay, silt, sand
Silt, sand, clay
Sand, clay, silt

why.correct: Sand grains are the largest (up to 2 mm), silt is medium, and clay particles are the smallest (less than 0.002 mm).
options: Right: sand is largest and clay smallest.
This is smallest to largest, the reverse order.
Sand grains are larger than silt.
Clay particles are smaller than silt.

items.q: Why does water drain through a sandy soil faster than through a clay soil?
options: Sand has large, connected pores that water flows through
Sand holds more humus, which pulls water down through the soil
Clay grains are larger, so they block the water from passing
Clay particles pack so tightly that clay has almost no pores

why.correct: Permeability depends on pore size. Large sand grains leave large, connected pores; tiny clay particles leave tiny pores that water moves through slowly.
options: Right: big, connected pores make sand highly permeable.
Humus does not pull water down; sand usually holds little humus.
Clay particles are the smallest, not the largest.
Clay has plenty of pore space, but its pores are tiny, so water moves slowly through them.

items.q: A gardener wants a soil that holds enough water for plants but still drains so roots get air. Which soil texture fits best?
options: Loam
Sand
Clay
Silty clay

why.correct: Loam mixes sand, silt and clay, so it combines enough drainage and air space with enough water-holding capacity and nutrients.
options: Right: loam balances drainage and water-holding capacity.
Sand drains so fast that it holds little water for plants.
Clay holds water but drains slowly, so roots can run short of air.
Silty clay is mostly fine particles, so it drains slowly too.

items.q: Why is a soil rich in clay and humus usually more fertile than a sandy soil?
options: Clay and humus hold nutrients against leaching
Clay and humus let water pass through faster than sand
Sand grains release substances that are toxic to roots
Clay and humus raise the temperature of the soil

why.correct: Tiny clay particles and humus have huge surface areas that hold nutrients, and humus releases nutrients as it decays. Water washes nutrients through sand quickly.
options: Right: clay and humus hold onto nutrients.
Clay and humus slow water down; sand drains fastest.
Sand is not poisonous; it just holds few nutrients.
Fertility is about nutrients, not soil temperature.

items.q: A soil test shows a field's soil has a pH of 4.5. What does this tell the farmer?
options: It is strongly acidic, which limits nutrients for many crops
It is close to neutral, which suits most crops very well
It is basic, so it will hold far too much water for crops
It is high in humus, so it needs little or no fertilizer

why.correct: A pH below 7 is acidic; 4.5 is strongly acidic. Most crops grow best near pH 6 to 7, and at low pH some nutrients become hard for roots to take up while some metals become more soluble.
options: Right: pH 4.5 is strongly acidic and limits nutrients.
Neutral is pH 7, not 4.5.
Basic soils have a pH above 7; pH also does not set how much water soil holds.
pH does not measure humus or fertility directly.

items.q: A soil sample is 35% sand and 45% silt. The rest is clay. What percent of the sample is clay?

why.correct: Sand, silt and clay add to 100%: $100\% - (35\% + 45\%) = 20\%$ clay. That sample is a loam.

mistakes.why: That is the sand and silt together (35 + 45). Clay is what is left: 100 - 80.
Subtract the sum of sand and silt from 100: 100 - (35 + 45) = 20.

items.q: On the triangle, which sample is a loam?
options: Sample B
Sample A
Sample C
Sample D

why.correct: Sample B (40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay) sits inside the shaded loam region in the middle of the triangle.
options: Right: B is in the loam region.
Sample A is in the sandy clay loam region.
Sample C is in the clay region at the top.
Sample D is in the silt loam region.

items.q: Sample D is 6% clay and 20% sand. What percent of sample D is silt?

why.correct: $100\% - (6\% + 20\%) = 74\%$ silt, which is why D sits in the silt loam region.

mistakes.why: That is the clay and sand together. Silt is the rest: 100 - 26 = 74%.
You subtracted 6 from 20. The three parts add to 100%: 100 - (6 + 20) = 74%.

items.q: Which sample would hold the most water but let water pass through it most slowly?
options: Sample C
Sample A
Sample B
Sample D

why.correct: Sample C is 60% clay. Clay's tiny pores hold water tightly and pass it slowly, so C has high water-holding capacity and low permeability.
options: Right: the clay sample holds water and drains slowly.
Sample A is 70% sand, so it drains quickly.
Sample B is a loam, in between.
Sample D is mostly silt with little clay, so it holds less water than C.

items.q: A town wants to build a sewage drain field, where wastewater soaks slowly into the soil, which needs soil that drains steadily. Which sample would cause the most trouble, and why?
options: Sample C: its tiny pores drain so slowly that water pools
Sample B: loam drains much too fast to filter the water
Sample A: sand holds water so tightly it barely drains
Sample D: silt has too little pore space for water to move

why.correct: A drain field needs water to soak in. Sample C, 60% clay, has low permeability, so wastewater would back up and pool.
options: Right: the clay sample has the lowest permeability.
Loam drains at a moderate rate, which suits a drain field.
Sand drains quickly; it does not hold water tightly.
Silt has pore space; it drains more slowly than sand but much faster than clay.

items.q: Which statement describes the data in the table?
options: Soils that drained more slowly held more water
Sand held the most water and also drained the most slowly
The three soils held roughly equal amounts of water
Clay drained the most water out of its column

why.correct: Clay took 50 minutes and held 110 mL; sand took 2 minutes and held 30 mL. Slow drainage and high water-holding go together.
options: Right: slow drainage goes with more water held.
Sand held the least water (30 mL) and drained fastest (2 minutes).
Water held ranged from 30 mL to 110 mL, a big difference.
Clay drained the least water out (90 mL).

items.q: The water in the loam column traveled 10 cm in 10 minutes. Find the percolation rate in centimeters per hour. Write the setup with units, then the answer. (1 hour = 60 minutes)

mistakes.why: Dividing by 60 again leaves min² on the bottom. Multiply by 60 min per hour so the minutes cancel.
A rate is distance over time; this puts time on top.
That is 1 cm per minute. The question asks per hour: multiply by 60.
You divided by 60. There are 60 minutes in an hour, so the water moves 60 times farther in an hour.

items.q: What percent of the 200 mL poured on the clay column did the clay hold?

mistakes.why: You left out the × 100. 110 ÷ 200 is 0.55, which is 55%.
That is the share that drained out (90 of 200). The clay held 110 of 200 mL.

items.q: Why did the class use the same depth of soil and the same 200 mL of water for every soil?
options: So any difference in drainage comes from the soil type
So that each soil would end up holding the same water
So that the sand would drain as slowly as the clay did
So the class could skip timing the water in each column

why.correct: Keeping depth and volume constant controls those variables. Then any difference in time or water held comes from the soil itself.
options: Right: constants let the class link the result to soil type.
The point is to see whether the soils differ, not to force them to be the same.
Constants do not change how a soil behaves; sand still drains fast.
The timing is the measurement; constants do not replace it.

items.q: Write a testable hypothesis for this experiment about clay content and drainage time.

why.correct: A hypothesis is a statement with a direction that names the variable measured: drainage time.

change.label: If
options: the clay content of the soil increases
more water is poured on the soil
the room is warmer

why.1: The volume of water was held constant at 200 mL.
why.2: Room temperature is not what the class changed.

variable.label: Then
options: the time for water to pass through the column
the depth of the soil column
the color of the soil

why.1: Depth was held constant at 10 cm.
why.2: The class measured time and volume, not color.

direction.label: Will
options: increase
be affected
change

why.1: "Be affected" does not say which way; a hypothesis gives a direction.
why.2: "Change" does not say which way; say increase or decrease.

specific.model: If the clay content of the soil increases, then the time for 200 mL of water to drain through a 10 cm column will increase.
